sections.heading: Heat is the product: why cooling defines a data center
bullets: Every watt a server draws becomes heat — a 100 MW data hall is a 100 MW heater running 24/7. The cooling plant's only job is moving that heat outdoors, and how it does so sets the facility's efficiency, water use, and maximum rack density

PUE (Power Usage Effectiveness) = total facility power ÷ IT power. A PUE of 1.5 means 50 extra MW of overhead per 100 MW of compute; every 0.1 saved is megawatts of pure cost avoided, around the clock, for decades

WUE (Water Usage Effectiveness) measures liters of water per kWh of IT. Traditional evaporative cooling literally boils away millions of gallons a year — increasingly the #1 reason communities veto data-center permits

The physics lever is delta-T: the temperature difference the cooling system works across. Capturing hot exhaust air at its hottest (a large delta-T) moves far more heat per fan-watt than mixing it into a room and chilling the lukewarm result

sections.heading: The air-cooling density wall
bullets: Classic design: CRAC/CRAH units along the walls push cold air under a raised floor, up through perforated tiles, through the servers, and back — effective at 5-15 kW per rack, strained above ~30 kW, broken by modern AI racks

Why it breaks: air carries little heat per unit volume, so doubling rack power means roughly doubling airflow — fan power grows with the cube of fan speed, and hot exhaust recirculating into intakes creates hotspots that force overcooling of the whole room
Conventional perimeter cooling works across only a 3-7°F effective exchange; the fans that force this can eat ~10% of the site's IT load by themselves
GPU racks now land at 50-150+ kW each and next-generation architectures push toward 600 kW-1 MW per rack — an order of magnitude past what room-scale air cooling was ever designed to move

sections.heading: Aligned's answer #1 — Delta³: capture heat at the source
bullets: Aligned's Delta³ (Delta Cube) inverts the classic model: instead of flooding the room with cold air, removable heat-sink arrays sit directly behind the racks and capture the hot exhaust at its hottest — working across a delta-T up to ~45°F instead of 3-7°F

Because the array works on hot, concentrated exhaust, fan work collapses: Aligned cites ~1% of IT load for fans vs ~10% for CRAC/CRAH rows, one moving part per array, and up to 50 kW per rack on air alone
The arrays are modular — cooling capacity is added rack-row by rack-row as the customer densifies, so a hall opened at low density never strands cooling capex ('slab to megawatts' scaling)

The heat is rejected through a closed water loop that never consumes water in operation (the loop is filled once) — the basis of the 'waterless' claim and the up-to-85%-less-water comparison vs conventional plants

sections.heading: Waterless heat rejection and the WUE weapon
bullets: Most large data centers reject heat evaporatively: cooling towers spray warm water through airflow, evaporation carries the heat away — cheap and efficient, but it consumes water permanently, at millions of gallons per year per site

The dry alternative: closed-loop fluid runs through finned coils (like a car radiator) and fans blow ambient air across them — zero water consumed, at the cost of more fan energy and reduced performance on the hottest days

A closed loop that never needs make-up water removes the community's most concrete objection — this is why 'zero water for operational cooling' features in Aligned's public commitments under Texas's 2026 data-center standards
Design consequence: waterless heat rejection unlocks sites in water-stressed, power-rich regions (West Texas, Arizona, Utah) that evaporative-cooled competitors struggle to permit

sections.heading: Aligned's answer #2 — DeltaFlow: one liquid spine, every cold-chain
bullets: Above ~50 kW per rack, air physically can't keep chips at temperature — coolant must touch the heat: cold plates bolted to GPUs (direct-to-chip), liquid-cooled rear doors, or full immersion tanks

DeltaFlow is Aligned's universal liquid platform: one facility technology-water/glycol loop (~65°F supply) that can feed direct-to-chip cold plates, rack-mounted CDUs (coolant distribution units — the heat exchanger + pumps between facility water and server loops), rear-door heat exchangers, and immersion pods

Rated at 350 kW of heat rejection per rack — about 2x what air alone delivers — and liquid is ~1000x more effective than air at carrying heat away from a surface, which is why the industry's transition is physics-driven, not fashion

Hybrid halls run Delta³ and DeltaFlow together for 600+ kW per rack combined rejection, and Aligned converts air halls to liquid in live operation with zero downtime — the 'ExpandOnDemand' pitch: your hall follows your chip roadmap instead of forcing a new building

sections.heading: Adaptive density: the economics of not knowing the future
bullets: Chip thermal design power roughly doubles every GPU generation — a hall designed rigidly for today's racks is obsolete mid-lease, and a hall overbuilt for tomorrow strands capital today

Aligned's Adaptive Modular Infrastructure standardizes the building shell and power spine while cooling modules (air arrays, liquid loops, hybrid) swap and scale within it — the data center as a chassis, not a fixed machine

This is a real financial instrument: a tenant can sign for a hall at 20 kW/rack and densify to 100+ kW/rack in place, so the landlord keeps the lease through multiple hardware refreshes instead of losing the tenant to a purpose-built site

An in-house test lab (Aligned's Advanced Cooling Lab, Phoenix) validates next-generation GPU thermals before field deployment — reducing the risk that 'liquid-ready' turns out to mean 'liquid-someday'

sections.heading: Build-to-scale: the wholesale landlord model
bullets: A wholesale data-center developer builds and owns the building, grid connection, and cooling plant; tenants (hyperscalers, GPU clouds, big enterprises) install their own IT under multi-year leases — the developer sells capacity and delivery speed, not computing

Product ladder: powered shell (structure + utilities, tenant fits out everything), dedicated data halls (finished space per tenant spec), and turnkey (fully fit-out). More finish = higher rent per MW = more landlord execution risk

'Build-to-scale' means construction phases track the tenant's expansion schedule — the tenant reserves growth capacity without paying for empty halls, and the developer builds against committed demand instead of speculation

Speed is the actual product: standardized designs, pre-provisioned supply chains, and repeatable campus playbooks compress delivery to months — decisive when a hyperscaler's alternative is a multi-year interconnection queue elsewhere

sections.heading: Power-first development: gigascale campuses and the queue problem
bullets: The binding constraint in AI buildout is no longer chips or land — it's grid interconnection: getting hundreds of megawatts approved and delivered can take longer than building the campus itself

'Power-first' development flips site selection: secure the land AND the utility power agreement before marketing the campus — powered land is the scarce asset; buildings are the easy part (Aligned's 540 MW Project Caprock in West Texas runs on dedicated utility infrastructure the developer itself funds)

Batteries as a queue-jumper: a campus-scale BESS (e.g., 31 MW / 62 MWh) lets the facility present itself to the grid as a flexible, curtailable load rather than a rigid one — utilities can approve flexible loads faster because they don't have to reinforce for the worst case

Brownfield conversion is the same logic in reverse: a retired coal-plant site (like Aligned's Conesville, Ohio campus) already has transmission-scale grid infrastructure — the queue was answered decades ago

sections.heading: Who owns the landlords: infrastructure capital and the $40B benchmark
bullets: Data centers fit the infrastructure-fund template: huge upfront capex, long contracted revenues from strong credits, and operating moats — so funds like Macquarie's buy platforms early, compound them for years, then exit to larger pools of capital (Macquarie entered Aligned at 85 MW in 2018 and sold a 5+ GW platform in 2026)

The scale-up is debt-engineered along the way: securitizations (bonds backed by the lease cash flows of specific campuses), sustainability-linked loans (margins tied to ESG targets), and private credit from insurance balance sheets — each layer priced against contracted rent, not corporate hope

The 2026 twist is WHO bought: AIP is a consortium whose members include the demand side itself (Microsoft, NVIDIA, xAI) alongside sovereign wealth (MGX/Abu Dhabi, Kuwait, Temasek) — compute buyers taking ownership of the landlord to secure their own capacity pipeline
A ~$40B enterprise value for a private developer resets the comp for every wholesale platform: the market is pricing proven multi-GW delivery capability and cooling IP, not just standing buildings

sections.heading: The competitive map: where Aligned sits
bullets: Private wholesale peers: Vantage, STACK, QTS (Blackstone), Switch, CyrusOne — all build-to-suit hyperscale landlords backed by mega-funds. Differentiation happens on power pipeline, delivery speed, and increasingly on liquid-cooling readiness

Aligned's distinct cards: proprietary cooling IP deployed platform-wide (peers largely integrate merchant Vertiv/Stulz/CDU equipment), waterless permitting advantage in dry states, and a four-country Latin America platform (ODATA) no US wholesale peer matches

Retail/interconnection colo (Equinix, Digital Realty's colo arm) is a different business: thousands of small tenants paying premium rates for network density — Aligned's multi-tenant offering is an on-ramp, not the model

In LatAm, the fight is against Ascenty (Digital Realty), Scala, and Equinix — and the moat is self-built power: ODATA energized its own substation capacity in Querétaro, making it Mexico's largest campus in a power-scarce market

flashcards.q: What do PUE and WUE measure, and why does each matter commercially?
flashcards.a: PUE = total facility power ÷ IT power (overhead efficiency — every 0.1 on 100 MW is ~10 MW of round-the-clock cost). WUE = water consumed per kWh of IT — the metric communities and permitting authorities increasingly veto projects over.

flashcards.q: Why does delta-T decide how efficient a cooling system can be?
flashcards.a: Heat moved scales with the temperature difference the system works across. Capturing exhaust at its hottest (~45°F delta-T) moves far more heat per fan-watt than perimeter CRAC/CRAH units mixing air into a room and working across 3-7°F.

flashcards.q: Why does conventional room-scale air cooling hit a wall around a few dozen kW per rack?
flashcards.a: Air carries little heat per volume, so power density demands cubic growth in fan energy, and recirculating hot exhaust creates hotspots that force overcooling the whole room. GPU racks at 50-150+ kW simply exceed what room air can move.

flashcards.q: How does Aligned's Delta³ array differ structurally from a CRAC/CRAH row?
flashcards.a: Instead of pushing cold air from the room perimeter, removable heat-sink arrays sit at the racks and capture hot exhaust at the source, rejecting it into a closed water loop — ~1% of IT load in fan power vs ~10%, one moving part, up to 50 kW/rack on air.

flashcards.q: What makes a cooling system 'waterless,' and what does it trade away?
flashcards.a: It rejects heat through closed-loop coils and dry coolers (filled once, never consumed) instead of evaporating water in cooling towers. It trades higher fan energy and tougher extreme-heat performance for zero operational water draw — and permits in water-stressed regions.

flashcards.q: What is a CDU and where does it sit in a liquid-cooled hall?
flashcards.a: A coolant distribution unit: the heat exchanger + pumps isolating the facility water loop from the server-side loop, delivering coolant at the right temperature/pressure to cold plates. It's the interface that lets one facility spine feed many rack technologies.

flashcards.q: Direct-to-chip vs rear-door vs immersion — what actually differs?
flashcards.a: Where liquid meets heat: cold plates bolted onto the chips (most heat captured at the die), a liquid heat exchanger on the rack's rear door (cools exhaust air), or servers submerged in dielectric fluid (everything wet). All can feed one technology-water loop.

flashcards.q: Why is liquid cooling a physics inevitability rather than a preference at AI densities?
flashcards.a: Liquid is roughly 1000x more effective than air at carrying heat off a surface. Once racks pass ~50 kW — and GPU roadmaps push toward 600 kW-1 MW — no achievable airflow keeps silicon at temperature; coolant must touch the heat source.

flashcards.q: What is a hybrid data hall and why do tenants value zero-downtime air-to-liquid conversion?
flashcards.a: A hall running air-cooled and liquid-cooled racks side by side on one infrastructure (Aligned cites 600+ kW/rack combined). Tenants refresh hardware every 2-3 years mid-lease — a hall that converts live follows the chip roadmap without a new building or a migration outage.

flashcards.q: Powered shell vs dedicated data hall vs turnkey — what's the ladder?
flashcards.a: Powered shell: structure + power/fiber, tenant builds the rest. Dedicated hall: finished space to tenant spec. Turnkey: fully fit-out, ready for racks. Each step up means higher rent per MW and more delivery risk carried by the landlord.

flashcards.q: What does 'build-to-scale' mean as a contract structure?
flashcards.a: Construction phases are sequenced to the tenant's committed expansion schedule — the tenant reserves future capacity without renting empty halls, and the developer builds each phase against contracted demand instead of speculating.

flashcards.q: Why has grid interconnection become the binding constraint in AI data-center development?
flashcards.a: Hundreds of megawatts of new load require utility studies, approvals, and often transmission reinforcement — timelines that can exceed construction itself. 'Powered land' (site + secured power agreement) is now the scarce, valuable asset.

flashcards.q: How does a campus-scale battery (BESS) accelerate a data center's grid connection?
flashcards.a: It converts the campus into a flexible, curtailable load: the battery covers peaks and lets the site reduce draw on command, so the utility can approve the connection without reinforcing the grid for the rigid worst case — buying years of queue time.

flashcards.q: Why do retired power-plant sites make attractive AI-campus locations?
flashcards.a: Transmission-scale grid infrastructure already exists and was permitted decades ago — the interconnection question is pre-answered. Brownfield conversion (like a former coal plant) trades demolition cost for queue-jumping and community goodwill.

flashcards.q: What is a data-center securitization (ABS) and what does its collateral disclosure reveal?
flashcards.a: Bonds backed by the lease cash flows of specific campuses rather than the corporate balance sheet. The collateral stats (customer count, share of rent from investment-grade tenants) are often the only tenant-quality data a private operator ever publishes.

flashcards.q: What is a sustainability-linked loan, and how does it differ from a green bond?
flashcards.a: An SLL prices the margin against company-level ESG targets (hit them, pay less) and the cash can be used generally; a green bond/securitization restricts proceeds to qualifying green assets under a verified framework. Aligned pioneered both in data centers.

flashcards.q: Why do infrastructure funds buy data-center platforms, and what does the exit look like?
flashcards.a: Huge upfront capex + long leases from strong credits + operating moats = infrastructure returns. The playbook: enter early (85 MW), fund the compounding buildout with layered debt, exit the multi-GW platform to a larger capital pool — Macquarie's 2018→2026 Aligned arc verbatim.

flashcards.q: What is structurally new about compute buyers (Microsoft, NVIDIA, xAI) sitting inside the consortium that owns a landlord?
flashcards.a: It vertically aligns demand with capacity: the parties who need gigawatts co-own the delivery machine, securing pipeline for themselves and signaling that AI capacity is strategic infrastructure — not just leasable real estate priced at arm's length.
